title: Neil Lawrence - Viable Systems, Judgment, and AI Safety

segments.text: NEIL LAWRENCE: So everything, everywhere, and all at once.
In Europe, sometimes it's something somewhere,
but not right now.
And bridging those two worlds is actually
at the heart of how we drive success.
And as you can probably tell from my accent,
I was born in New Jersey--
or should I say New Jersey, but live in the UK.
And Trent is a company that straddles those worlds.
So what I want to talk to you about
is what AI safety is looking like on the ground
and for customers.
And what we see is it's an accountability problem.
And I don't mean accountability in the great way
Lovedeep was talking about it.
I mean, it's an accountability problem,
and people have to stand up and say, I'm signing that off.
That's my responsibility.
I don't know what the world's going
to be like in 10 years' time.
I can't tell you what's going to happen,
but I can tell you what's not going to happen.
That is not going away.
Lovedeep mentioned two of the areas, finance and clinical.
But that's not just coming from the EU AI Act.
That's coming from customers.
That's coming from enterprise customers, people who are not
willing to risk their business on the back of AI agents
they don't understand.
And that comes through in this quote that I stick with.
Accounting is in the numbers.
Accountability is in the human authority and the judgment.
And the challenge we face is computers
do accounting very, very well, but they don't do accountability
well.
They are not socially accountable.
They can't be sent to jail.
They can't be embarrassed.
They can't lose their job.
And our society is entirely based
on that form of accountability.
But if you separate the human accounts
from the accountability, you put the human in a situation
where they don't understand the accounts
and they can't stand up for accountability.
And that's the gap we've got to bridge.
So what that means is we put ourselves in a position
where we devolve authority without judgment.
So what do I mean by that?
Well, there's an amazing theorem that
comes from 1970 called the good regulator theorem.
It's Roger Conant and Ross Ashby.
And the theorem says the following thing.
If I'm going to delegate authority,
if I'm going to delegate authority,
I have to have a good model-- it's called the good regulator
theorem--
I have to have a good model of the entity I'm
delegating authority to.
So if I tell an intern to make me coffee,
I have to have a good sense that the intern's
going to do that sensibly, that they're not
going to go away and hack the NSA to get the optimal coffee
recipe.
They're just going to make me a coffee.
It also works the other way.
The delegatee has to have a good model
of who's delegating to them so they
know when to surface problems.
The machine's run out of coffee.
I don't know how to deal with that, whatever it is.
And this is the challenge with accountability and agentic AI.
Because if you're delegating authority
to a model that is so large and so big
that you don't understand how it's going to solve the problem,
you're stuffed.
And we genuinely see that in the problems that are arising.
You cannot delegate authority in that way.
So what we have to do is avoid that situation,
because it creates what we call agentic debt.
If you build that into your workflow systems in companies,
you are storing up downstream trouble.
You don't understand how your own systems are operating.
And that's what we're working on at Trent.
So instead of replacing engineers-- and in this case,
our focus is cybersecurity.
Because when we set up, initially, our first thinking
was we knew that was going to be the first front of this problem.
And when we go into companies, they say,
we don't want you to do our cybersecurity for us.
We want you to support our security engineers
in doing their job, because they're becoming overwhelmed,
as we've just seen with Apple switching off their bug bounty
system.
And those are the people that are
accountable within those businesses.
So when we build agentic AI systems,
we can use agentic AI systems to support security engineers.
What we cannot do is go in and say,
here's a system you don't understand and you've never seen
before, and you now have to sign it off.
You have to take responsibility that you can deploy.
That's absolutely disastrous.
And the way you bridge the world between everything
all at once and not here, not now, is by talking to customers.
And one challenge we're seeing in agentic AI
is not enough of that.
So when we deploy, we have to remember,
accountability is king.
And with that, I'm finished.
Thank you.
